To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
there is no free lunch in learning, and that the price of generality is inescapable deficiencies in the programs that can be learned.

(1) there are learning devices that, thanks to a small increase in their generality, can provably learn some optimal programs in polynomial time, but, still because of the increased generality, cannot learn other optimal programs in polynomial space, and (2) there are learning machines that can provably learn optimal programs in polynomial-time, but, because of their generality, cannot provably learn the fact that the programs learned by them are optimal, even though that fact is provably true
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: (1) What are the tradeoffs between the quality of programs learned by a machine and the generality of the learning device?
the question, "How much can we learn from data?"
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, thanks to the generally applicable, algorithmic nature of the learning device, some of the learned programs are provable, algorithmically unalterable, suboptimal or information deficient, but the learning device is nevertheless provably optimal, as to its own generality, and the programs that are provably optimal, are provably information deficient.
, inescapably, there is a price to be paid in terms of program complexity and/or program quality for the generality of a machine learning device.
generality of a device is a price that must be paid in order to have it learn provably good programs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that there is no free lunch in machine learning: if we want to learn programs of high quality, we have to pay a price in the form of generality of the learning device.
we have discovered a few more examples of the phenomenon that, in some cases, generality has a price.
we have found that, in the context of learning, generality is not free.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the complexity of programs learned by a machine-learning device is not always a reliable indicator of their quality, and, in some cases, it is not even possible to tell, algorithmically, that they are even close to optimal.
the complexity of a program is not just a function of its own algorithmic description, but is also influenced by the complexity of the learning device which produced the program.
the complexity-theoretic limitations of the learning process itself can be as severe as the limitations of the learned programs.
